speakeroldname: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just returned from Washington where I had the honour of heading the Canadian delegation at the spring ministerial meeting of the North Atlantic council. I think the house might be interested to receive a brief report regarding those meetings. First I should like to pass on to you, Mr. Speaker, and the other members of the house the many messages of sympathy which were expressed by his former colleagues, the various foreign secretaries of the NATO countries, with regard to the untimely death of Dr. Sidney Smith.
The meeting I attended was an important one in that the members of the alliance were confronted with a serious challenge as a result of the Soviet union's recent pronouncement concerning Berlin and Germany. It also assumed special significance because it marked the tenth anniversary of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization which came into being on April 4, 1949. In this regard the opening ceremonies, which were attended by the President of the United States, were held in the same hall where the treaty had originally been signed.
At that first meeting, coinciding as it did with a tense international situation, a group of freedom-loving nations decided to join efforts against the danger of aggression. The prospect then of further encroachment on the free world seemed imminent. Those who drafted the treaty believed this danger could be averted only if it were made clear to the Soviet union that an attack on any of the members of the North Atlantic alliance would be regarded as an attack on all of them.
The events of the past ten years have proved the soundness of that policy. Had it not been for the North Atlantic treaty there might well have been further losses of people and territories to the Soviet empire. Indeed, the whole defensive position of the west might have been desperate. We should be grateful to the men of many nations who negotiated the treaty and secured its acceptance. Expressions of gratitude were given at the opening meeting of the sessions I have just attended.
2344	HOUSE OF
NATO-Report on Washington Meeting
We can take satisfaction from the way in which over the years NATO has gained strength. Mr. Spaak, the chairman and secretary general of the North Atlantic council, in his opening remarks had this to say:
Ten years ago the North Atlantic treaty gave practical expression to the union of twelve countries and to their common determination to resist any active aggression. Today this union and this determination appear to us so natural and so necessary that we can no longer conceive for our peoples a free and peaceful existence without them.
Modes of consultation have been developed in which all member nations can freely express their views on the common problems. They received the opportunity of expressing those views in the three-day meetings in Washington. As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister in his statement of April 7 has already given an account of the position taken by Canada on the principal questions discussed at the Washington meetings. These were primarily concerned with the German problems.
It is unnecessary for me to elaborate on what the Prime Minister has said, though I would call attention to the statement he made about the suggestion which was advanced by the Canadian delegation that in some manner the United Nations might be able to assist in the solution of the Berlin problem. In the House of Commons on March 19 the Prime Minister expressed the belief that the United Nations might play some significant role in the solution of the Berlin problem, and that this suggestion deserved further and more careful study.
Further study has been given to the possibility of the United Nations playing some part, and suggestions were made at the meeting as to how the United Nations might contribute something to the solution of the problem. I pointed out that we in Canada were anxious that consideration be given to ways by which the present arrangements over Berlin could be strengthened, either by supplementary or substitute arrangements. I pointed out that the Prime Minister had made his statement as of March 19, and then I went on to say that I would doubt if the United Nations could play a useful part unless a four-power agreement had first been reached. I suggested that a settlement involving the United Nations need not be weaker, and conceivably might be more stable, than the present position in which the powers are now in Berlin by right of conquest. Although the effective introduction of the United Nations into the Berlin situation could probably be accomplished only through the agreement of the four powers, it could


serve to engage the interest of other governments in the freedom and independence of Berlin in a way which no agreement reached solely among the occupying powers could do. Accordingly I suggested it would be worth while for the permanent council to study the possibilities of a role for the United Nations in the application of a solution to the Berlin problem, and an assurance was given that a full study would be made by the permanent council of the suggestions which were put forward.
The two main suggestions which I advanced were, first, that the basic role of the United Nations might be to verify that all parties were abiding by the terms of whatever agreement was reached; and, second, that an essential part of the agreement would be a Soviet pledge binding itself and its associates to permit full freedom of access to West Berlin and the acceptance of a United Nations presence on the lines of communication.
I think all hon. members will appreciate that at this very moment the western powers having special responsibility-the United States, the United Kingdom, France and Germany-after receiving the advice of the allies at the NATO conference, are now preparing for the negotiations which lie ahead, and that great restraint should be exercised and nothing said which might make those negotiations even more difficult. I am satisfied that the views presented by myself on behalf of the Canadian government will be given the most serious consideration by the experts in the series of consultations now scheduled to take place before the foreign ministers' meeting on May 11.
I can report to the house that the unity which marked the council's adoption of its declaration on Berlin last December also characterized the meetings in Washington last week. All 15 nations which were represented expressed their conviction that "the unity of action and policy which the alliance makes possible is the best guarantee of successful negotiations with the Soviet government and of any genuine resolution of differences between east and west".
In addition to the extensive discussion of the problems of Germany and Berlin, the council directed its attention to the political situation in other parts of the world where international communism continues to exert various forms of pressure on the free world. In the Canadian view it is a cause for gratification that during the last year or so there has been a marked increase in consultation among the governments of the alliance in respect of these problems which lie outside the area covered by the treaty. Because the

pressure exercised by the communist bloc is not limited to the countries of the alliance or confined to direct military aggression, the council is obliged to look beyond the territorial boundaries of the treaty in order to prevent encroachment on freedom in other parts of the world.
I am also convinced that in spite of difficulties it is possible to achieve a high degree of harmony in national policies within the present treaty commitments and, without giving ground for misunderstanding, in other areas of the free world.
There was also a useful discussion of the work of the alliance during the past year. The council endorsed the secretary general's report calling for a further impetus to be given to the work of the alliance and recognizing the need for increased collective action in regard not only to political consultation and the common defence effort, but also to certain aspects of economic, scientific and cultural matters.
Canada and the other countries have now had the opportunity to express their views on the problems of Berlin and Germany. The four powers who will be directly involved in the forthcoming negotiations with the Soviet union are fully aware of our views.
I am confident that those who are representing these powers will prove equal to the challenge of the tasks they have ahead.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister's statement has proven to be an interesting and valuable supplement to that given yesterday by the Prime Minister on the work of the recent NATO council meeting in Washington. It is, I believe, all the more welcome because it is, if I may say so, more informative than the communique which was issued at the end of the council session. I believe that all hon. members of this house and indeed all Canadians as well as the great majority of citizens in all the Atlantic countries have real cause for satisfaction in the fact that NATO has been able to celebrate its 10th birthday.
The minister mentioned the origin of NATO and those who were responsible for its foundation. I am thinking in that connection especially of four men who did not take part in the ceremony in Washington. I am thinking of John Foster Dulles, who had so much to do with the development of the coalition and who was kept away because of illness. I am thinking, too, of Dean Acheson, who was one of the really effective founders of NATO. I am also thinking of Chancellor Adenauer, a great champion of freedom, who has decided to withdraw soon from active participation in
8,	1959	2345
NATO-Report on Washington Meeting domestic and international affairs. I am thinking also of the former prime minister of this country, Louis St. Laurent, who was one of the first leaders of an Atlantic government to give public expression to the desirability and indeed the necessity of building up an Atlantic community not merely for defence but for development.
We have been successful in these ten years in developing NATO into an effective organization for collective defence, though no doubt its strategy in that regard will have to be changed in the next ten years as it faces new problems in the field of defence. We have not been so successful, as we all know, in building up NATO as an effective agency for development. Perhaps in the years ahead the greatest tests that NATO will meet will be in the field of building up the Atlantic community for purposes other than military defence, to which the minister made reference this afternoon; in the field of co-ordinating foreign policy and economic policy. If NATO cannot make progress in that regard it will undoubtedly disappear as a coalition with the disappearance of the danger and the fear that gave rise to NATO in the first place. And so, as we look ahead to the next ten years, I think all in this house agree that it will be an important aspect of Canadian policy to do what can be done to build up NATO in this respect.
The minister mentioned one test that is immediately before NATO; that is the test which it faces in the settlement of the Berlin and German questions. I quite agree with him; and, as was indicated yesterday, if this problem, so important to the peace of Europe, is to be solved it is desirable to broaden the basis of responsibility for West Berlin from the four occupying powers to all the NATO powers, and to use the NATO council for that and other purposes as an effective agency for negotiation.
I was glad to hear the minister say that he thinks in the last year real progress has been made in that regard. In any steps the Canadian government can take to support that progress I assure the minister and I assure the government they will get full support from this side of the house.

Mr. Speaker, we believe that NATO in the last 10 years has effectively served the interests of the peace of the world. We believe that NATO, with the emphasis that has been given to it, should be greatly changed at this time. NATO has been basically a defensive and a military organization. At a time when people agree that many nations in the world have weapons capable of bringing about world destruction there should be a re-examination of NATO

itself, of the things that have been accomplished under NATO, and an examination to see how we can best proceed.
We are most happy with the emphasis that has been given to the desirability of the United Nations itself playing a greater role in Europe and in questions of peace vis-a-vis the United States, the Soviet union, the North Atlantic organization and the eastern bloc. For many years we have looked for greater emphasis on economic co-operation. The C.C.F. have been greatly disappointed in that so little emphasis has been given to clause II of the agreement. The whole question of Berlin is very much to the fore, and we are hopeful that arrangements will be made to maintain the freedom of West Berlin but at the same time to bring about a withdrawal of troops within central Europe and the strengthening of peaceful relations among the nations involved.
As the foreign ministers' conference approaches, and as the NATO nations are about to go into the consultations to which the minister referred, we feel that this lends emphasis to the need for Canada to be fully represented by the Prime Minister immediately appointing a person to occupy the position of Secretary of State for External Affairs.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: R.C.M.P. REINFORCEMENTS, NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall answer the two questions at one time. I do have to refer to question 47 as well. I shall answer it in view of the fact that I undertook to do so, although I do not wish the answer in any way to constitute a precedent, for I believe the question is in derogation of the rule set out in citation 171 (p), Beauchesne's fourth edition, which says:
No questions must be asked which might prejudice a pending trial in a court of law.
The pertinent words in the telegram from the premier of Newfoundland are as follows:
The attorney general of Newfoundland informs me that the Minister of Justice of Canada has cancelled temporarily the dispatch of 50 additional officers of the R.C.M.P. for duty in the present emergency in central Newfoundland. Newfoundland has a solemn contract with the Canadian government, identical with those signed by Canada with seven other provinces.
Then it says, after some intermediate words:
I now ask you to supply us with the additional R.C.M.P. men to enable us to maintain law and order in this emergency according to the contract that exists between us. If you cannot or will not do so will you undertake to have the government of Canada take over the task of maintaining law and order in central Newfoundland. If you will not give us the police to do it as the contract requires you to do then will you take on the responsibility yourselves of maintaining law and order in this emergency.
Then in the other telegram the pertinent parts are:
In the interest of the peace, order and good government of Canada and to protect the good name of the R.C.M.P. the government of Newfoundland invites the government of Canada to set up at once a public inquiry under a superior court judge from outside Newfoundland to investigate the acts of lawlessness and violence which have taken place in central Newfoundland since the strike of the loggers began on December 31 for the purpose of ascertaining the facts and assessing the responsibility.

Those are the pertinent words. There are, of course, additional ones. To both these telegrams I replied:
I find I have not replied formally for the record to your telegrams of March 12 and 13.
The pertinent words are these:
You will, of course, he aware that the government gave most serious and urgent consideration to the requests in your telegrams. In view of the widespread public interest in the matter it was necessary for us to make public our stand on this proposal in parliament just as quickly as the legislation was ready. I stated the position of the government in parliament on Monday March 16. I understand that you learned of this decision almost immediately when announced. X am sending you, for your records, a copy of the statement taken from the official record of our debates.
Then I concluded:
I feel it would be out of place for me to add anything to that statement.

He pointed out that the difficulty-the major difficulty-which was responsible for his not proceeding with the measure was that he himself, so he said, would not like to take responsibility for appointing a parliamentary assistant or a parliamentary secretary without consultation and agreement with the minister of the department concerned, and that he found the ministers of various departments were most reluctant to choose from among the members of parliament one who might become an assistant.

I call to the attention of the Prime Minister that if this gave rise to a difficulty in those days, that difficulty has certainly been compounded by one clause of this bill, which would put the Prime Minister and the ministers in this difficult position every year. But I shall have more to say about this later, when we come to the committee stage.
Meanwhile I reaffirm what we said when we were discussing the resolution, namely that we shall support the principle of this bill, without prejudice to any observations we may wish to make or any changes we may wish to see introduced when we discuss the bill in committee.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to make provision for a maximum of some 16 parliamentary secretaries. This parliament during one whole session and for a substantial part of another session has operated in the absence of parliamentary secretaries, and I think those of us who


have had some experience in the House of Commons will agree that our experience without parliamentary secretaries has demonstrated the wisdom of this present bill. Many of the cabinet ministers are overworked. They have great burdens, and they need help. There may be a few of them-I can think of a couple-who perhaps are not fully employed, but we realize that many of the portfolios are very heavy and very trying. The provision of parliamentary secretaries would, we believe, be of help to the government, and consequently would lead to the more efficient dispatch of public business.
I am sure there are many ways in which parliamentary secretaries could be helpful to a minister. One such way would be in seeing that questions of which hon. members have given advance notice to a minister are taken to the proper authorities in the appropriate department and the answers obtained. In that way we would obtain greater efficiency in the answering of questions in this house. There have been in this session instances of questions being asked and the replies requiring many weeks before being prepared and presented.
I can think of other ways in which parliamentary secretaries would be of assistance. I think that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is greatly in need of a parliamentary secretary. We realize that his portfolio is particularly heavy and that in the past ministers of this department have made great use of their parliamentary secretaries. As a matter of fact, this type of service has been a training ground in some instances for a person who subsequently became the minister of that portfolio. While I believe the major business of parliament should be conducted by the ministers themselves, I can appreciate that parliamentary secretaries may be able to give parliament more adequate answers on many important questions when the ministers are busy with other matters.
To cite another example, parliamentary secretaries would be useful when supplementary estimates are before the house. The secretary may be able to provide appropriate answers. This would depend on the individual himself and the extent to which he had been briefed with regard to questions that might be asked.
I believe that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) could do with a parliamentary secretary. He might, for instance, use him to open letters containing complaints. The minister said he has received no complaints about box car allocation, a comment I was interested in hearing. I would like to see a parliamentary secretary assigned to the Minister of Trade and Commerce who would keep him informed on these

questions and complaints. The minister today seemed not to have any great knowledge about the importation of canned apples. This perhaps illustrates his need of a parliamentary secretary.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) who is the government leader in the house is an efficient person and in my opinion handles his department extremely well but I feel he would benefit from the assistance of a parliamentary secretary to handle in this house the strategy as far as private members' days are concerned. The parliamentary secretary to the house leader might be able to bring about some arrangement that would give parliament an opportunity to deal in a more effective manner with the whole question of private members' motions and private members' bills. Perhaps we could discover an alternative to the usual course of talking out all of these motions.
In the field of policy it would appear to me that the minister of as important a department as the Department of Labour might make use of a parliamentary secretary to make inquiries into the grave unemployment problem confronting the nation to see what might be done about solving it.
I suggest that the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) should have a parliamentary secretary to keep track of royal commissions, how long they take to report and what they are doing.

A former parliamentary assistant tells me that there is no man made who could accomplish such a task. One royal commission that could be inquired into with respect to the progress it is making is the royal commission on patents and copyrights. This commission has been sitting for many years and parliament would be interested in knowing when a report may be expected.
There is no question about it, the growing complexity of the role of the Canadian government in our economy requires a strengthening of administration from time to time.
I am certain that an investment of this relatively small amount of money for this purpose is a good investment for the nation.

I am quite sure that the Prime Minister must have had good reason for postponing this legislation; but as one reads the bill he immediately realizes that the Prime Minister is actually increasing the number of parliamentary secretaries from 14 to 16 and that he is making his appointments for a period not exceeding one year. I must confess, Mr. Speaker, I cannot help but recall the very nasty rumours and stories that were circulated around parliament hill some time ago to the effect that there were


some 180 hungry and eager parliamentarians who were very anxious to get away from the rank and file of the Conservative party and that the Prime Minister had a bit of a problem in trying to fit 180 members into the 14 available positions. As a matter of fact, he was seriously considering appointing the parliamentary secretaries on an annual rotation basis so that he might, of course, satisfy as many of his political colleagues as possible. Now that the bill has been brought down and we see its provisions we also realize that the rumours that we have heard were not entirely without foundation. At this time we should have a very definite look at the consequences of this particular legislation and not let ourselves be sidetracked into considerations of Mr. King's procrastinations in this matter.
I think I should make it clear, Mr. Speaker, right from the start that I am not opposed to the appointment of parliamentary secretaries. On the contrary, I feel that at a time when most of the government departments have expanded to an unprecedented level and where the ministers are literally overburdened with departmental administration, policies and detail; when they must look after not only the affairs in this house but must also study the problems that may come before the cabinet; when they are called upon to represent the government not only from coast to coast in this country but also abroad, there is absolute need for the appointment of knowledgeable parliamentary assistants, and it would be in the greatest interest of parliament if the parliamentary assistants were to be named because of their capacity rather than for any other criteria.
Since 1943, when the parliamentary assist-antships were set up on a more definite and more permanent basis, than had been the case heretofore, I believe they have rendered valuable service to the house and to parliament. I am sure the experiment has been a considerable success. It has been proven to be a good training ground for members of parliament and indeed has been a stepping stone to the cabinet. However, I believe the time has now come when parliamentary assistants should be given a new status in the hierarchy of the departments. They should be given more definite and specific responsibilities in the departments to which they are attached and in the performance of their duties in this house in order to lessen as effectively as possible the burden which is now on the shoulders of the ministers alone.
There is no doubt in my mind, Mr. Speaker, that there are innumerable members on the government side who would make exceedingly fine parliamentary assistants provided, of

course, that they were chosen for their capacity, their training and their adaptability and provided that they are not chosen in an effort to make content as many of the government members as possible. I think indeed it would be a very gross disregard of the rights of parliament as well as of the rights of the Canadian taxpayers to use parliamentary secretaries as a means of recompensing the supporters of the government.
At this stage of our political evolution, there is an absolute need in parliament and in the departments for good parliamentary secretaries. These responsibilities should fall on the shoulders of the most qualified men. I shall even go farther, Mr. Speaker: If the parliamentary secretaries are to play the role that is required in this house and in the departments then I submit respectfully that these should be full-time jobs. If that is so, then I believe serious consideration should be given to increasing the amount of the emolument that is now provided for in this bill.
I do not believe $4,000 is sufficient for a full-time job. We should not expect capable men, who no doubt have family obligations, to neglect or completely abandon for a period of two or three years whatever business they have without assuring them of an adequate return for the services they render. On the other hand, if parliamentary assistants are to be named on a yearly rotation basis, then I submit that this type of political pie-cutting is out of keeping with the very purpose for which parliamentary secretaries were instituted in the first place. I am quite sure all hon. members will agree that it would take a considerably longer period than six or seven months or a year for a person to be fully acquainted with and knowledgable of the details of his department. It would take a considerably longer period than that, and by changing and rotating parliamentary secretaries from year to year you would place the parliamentary secretary in a position where he could be of no possible use to the department, to the minister or to the house. As a matter of fact, that type of parliamentary secretary would be occupying a purely honorary position. I believe that the moneys that would be expended in payment for that type of parliamentary secretary would be wasted. As a matter of fact, what you would be asking the Canadian people to do would be to pay the government's debt of gratitude to some members of the Conservative party.
In addition I feel that although this legislation may call for the appointment of 16 parliamentary secretaries the Prime Minister would not be justified in filling these 16 positions in order to satisfy as many of his colleagues as possible. I do not think it would be reasonable or even logical, for instance, to
8, 1959	2357
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries name a parliamentary assistant to the attorney general or to the ministers without portfolio or to any of the departments in which the work involved does not justify the naming of a parliamentary assistant. In my opinion, there is a need for good parliamentary assistants, and they should be placed in those departments in which it is well known the minister is overburdened; where there is a quantity of important detail which the minister has not the time to handle and which could be well handled by a good parliamentary secretary.
It would be, I am sure, in the interests of the departments, of the ministers and of this house to place the best available men in these key positions. This is the only basis upon which we can support, and even heartily endorse, the appointment of parliamentary secretaries. This is the only basis upon which the Prime Minister could justify the appointment of parlamentary secretaries if he desires, as he said, to preserve the rights and dignity of parliament and to improve our parliamentary procedures. I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the appointment of parliamentary secretaries on an annual rotation basis would, in fact, destroy the effectiveness of parliamentary assistants, and although that procedure may be of some definite political advantage to the Conservative party, I submit such a course would be contrary to the best interests of this parliament.

I am sure those who are now in the house are anxiously awaiting the passage of this bill to ascertain whether or not they will be reappointed. For my part, I wish it were possible for the Prime Minister to appoint every member of his party as a parliamentary secretary, so well disposed do I feel toward every hon. member who sits on the Speaker's right.
Notwithstanding that, the situation is that there were parliamentary assistants appointed after the election of June, 1957. They functioned, I think one may say, with competence and with distinction, and served their ministers and their country well. During the period of their appointment the Prime Minister, however, decided, according to his prerogative as the Queen's first minister, by his request for dissolution, to bring to an end the tenure of the parliamentary assistants who were associated with his government. This long delay since January, 1958 has not been explained properly by the Prime Minister. If there is justification, as I believe there is, for the appointment of parliamentary assistants, or as the bill calls them, secretaries, at this time, there certainly was justification for the Prime Minister taking this step shortly after his return to office on March 31, 1958.
What the reasons for the delay were, of course, I do not know. I have not yet reached that point of efficiency as to be able to satisfactorily and confidently detect what is in the mind of the right hon. gentleman. However, one suspects, as in the case of most prime ministers, that there was real difficulty, difficulty that arises out of dissatisfaction on the part of some hon. gentlemen who were not previously appointed, and possibly some dissatisfaction-but I am sure that could not have existed in many cases-with the record of achievement of parliamentary assistants previously designated, although, as I say, I do not know of anyone who was a parliamentary assistant after June of 1957 who could not qualify under the highest standards.
It may be that the Prime Minister has since found that certain political obligations have now confronted him which he is obliged to take into consideration. It would be


regrettable if now, in the appointment of new candidates, he would do what the hon. member who has just spoken said he should not do, namely make appointments on the basis of trying to extricate himself from particular inevitable political embarrassments that attend the head of any government. One would hope that the Prime Minister could find some other method of dealing with these political embarrassments or these potential dissatisfactions and that he would appoint as parliamentary secretaries only those men in his party who sit behind him in whom he has the fullest confidence and whom he regards as most competent for the particular assignments.
The hon. member for Assiniboia points out that I am now discriminating by failing to mention not only those sitting behind the Prime Minister but as well those members of his party who sit opposite. Because I have carefully observed an attitude of complete neutrality on these appointments I would want to include all hon. members sitting on this side of the house who support the right hon. gentleman. I am sure that our propinquity with these hon. members over the period of the last few months has given us a special opportunity of recognizing their high qualifications for these junior ministerial positions. Of course, as the Leader of the Opposition quietly observes, in their propinquity with us they have had an opportunity of adding to their standards, competence and qualifications.
I hope the Prime Minister will take into account another factor that is extremely important in this matter and it is this. While there has been in this country a tradition about trying to give cabinet representation to all sections of the country, and particularly to the divisions within a province, and while I recognize that that is a rule to be observed by the Prime Minister in accordance with his own prerogative and his own concepts of the kind of government he wants, the Prime Minister now has, in the particular appointments which will be open to him once this bill is passed, the opportunity of rectifying some of the weaknesses that attend the present ministry.
For instance, in the province of Ontario the Prime Minister has a group of respectably competent gentlemen who sit on the ministerial benches, including the distinguished lady member from Hamilton. I have no observations to make against any one of those particular ministers and I would not want them to think that I was in any way engaged in a campaign to have them withdrawn by attrition, compulsion or persuasion from the right hon. gentleman's government. But for

Mr. Chairman, I rise briefly to express the support of this group for this measure because we believe that under present conditions parliamentary secretaries are necessary and can render a service to parliament and a service to the public. Before going on with my few remarks, I do want to deal with the obvious inconsistencies between various members of the Liberal party who have spoken in this debate. We had the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River pleading with the Prime Minister not to adopt the British practice and call them parliamentary secretaries. Then we had the hon. member for Essex East who has just taken his seat criticizing another section of the bill and wondering why the Prime Minister did not adopt the British practice in this respect. I might say, Mr. Chairman, that we in this group are quite willing, when it comes to the procedures and operations of the parliamentary system, to receive our instruction from the mother of parliaments in Great Britain. They have had long experience and their practices have been proven worth while throughout the years.
We do hope that the Prime Minister will give consideration to competence, not to geographical regions and things of that sort. Secondly, we hope he will give consideration to youth. While possibly out of a spirit of humanitarianism it may be necessary to

consider a few gray heads, we would not object to that so long as the number was not more than four out of sixteen. We do think that young men should get the opportunity to serve in these positions. I think, generally speaking, that parliamentary secretaryships are looked upon as training grounds for cabinet positions at a later date, and I think the young men should have their opportunity to show their competence in this respect.
There are a few questions which I trust the Prime Minister will answer when he replies to the criticism on section 1. We in this group would like to know what rank these parliamentary secretaries will hold. In Great Britain they are treated as junior ministers, and there is a provision in their table of precedence for parliamentary secretaries. There is no such provision in our table of precedence, and I would like to know whether there will be consideration given to that. What are their duties? While the bill particularly mentions that they shall assist the minister in such manner as the minister directs, we in this group would like to know more specifically what is expected of them with respect to assisting the minister and with respect to their duties in the house, and just what opposition members can expect from them by way of assistance. I know that parliamentary secretaries can be of great assistance to a minister and save a lot of his time by providing an opportunity for members to take up their questions with them outside the house and on other occasions. We would like a more detailed explanation of their duties.
In addition, will they be required to resign any directorships, the same as a minister? That is the practice in Great Britain, and seeing that the Prime Minister has followed fairly well the practice which prevails in Great Britain in the drafting of this bill, surely he will insist on that. We in this group are glad that the bill provides for appointments for only one year. We are all human beings and it gives persons appointed as parliamentary secretaries some opportunity for initiative. They are not just appointed and then go on till the end of the parliament. They have to demonstrate their ability not only to the Prime Minister but to the rest of the house, and we think that is an excellent provision. It provides an opportunity for the Prime Minister to drop any duds, not that I am suggesting that he will appoint duds, but it is the sort of thing which could possibly happen.
That is all I have to say at this stage. I hope the Prime Minister will give some fuller explanation of the questions other hon. members and I have asked.

Thus, in fact, it was an appointment from year to year. The question was asked: why the expression "parliamentary secretary"? I adopted the view of Mr. King, and this was his first thought on the subject in 1935. Then I read the British practice, and I was particularly impressed with the book written by the Right Hon. Mr. Herbert Morrison on the British parliament and the general system, and it was on that basis that the alteration was made.
The hon. member for Kootenay West asked whether the parliamentary secretaries are to be given the status of junior ministers, and without any qualification in this regard I say that they are not. We have today a different system from that which exists in the United Kingdom. There, in effect, the ministry consists of two grades-those in the cabinet and those outside the cabinet. Originally, in 1917 or 1918 when Sir Robert Borden introduced this system into the House of Commons here, he did have in mind that parliamentary secretaries-which, incidentally, was the name then given to those hon. members, few in number as they were, who were appointed to those positions-might on occasion sit in the cabinet. At the moment my colleagues and I have no favourable views in that regard.
In so far as tables of precedence are concerned, may I say to the hon. member for Kootenay West that tables of precedence are one thing that have never been of particular concern for me. As a matter of fact I do not know how they are determined; perhaps the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, having occupied the various positions that he has in the civil service and having, also, been secretary of state, would be able to enlighten hon. members on this point. All I know is that it is in the red book. Who determines it, I do not know. I can say that as far as parliamentary secretaries are concerned, there is no suggestion of precedence other than that during the course of the discharge of their responsibilities in the House of Commons and outside they will on appropriate occasions as the minister directs perform those duties which are in essence comprehended by the expression "parliamentary secretary".
A question was raised by one hon. member-I think it was the hon. member for Kootenay West-as to whether parliamentary secretaries would be required to divest themselves of directorships in companies. I have always been a strong believer in the necessity of members of a cabinet being divested of any interest in any corporation, by which I mean, not the interest of a shareholder in the various companies in which one


might buy shares but an interest as a director of any corporation. I think that has been generally accepted, although some years ago when there was a discussion of this question in the house the then prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, as I recall, while he himself had divested himself of all interest in this regard and felt, personally, that such a course should be followed, acknowledged that one minister or another did hold certain directorships.
I am speaking from recollection but I believe Mr. St. Laurent said it was a question for the individual to determine. I believe those occupying positions in the cabinet should, without question, divest themselves of that kind of interest. That is the view I hold. In so far as parliamentary secretaries are concerned the line is much finer but I believe that in the general interests of the preservation of the parliamentary system in its entirety, and the assurance that no consideration other than the determination of the responsibilities of the member shall enter into the equation, parliamentary secretaries should follow a similar course.
The Leader of the Opposition dealt in general with the matter and I thank him for his remarks and for the general support that has been expressed. There may be some questions that will arise later on as the various clauses come up for consideration.
The hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres thought there should be an increase in the amount of $4,000 to be paid as remuneration. I know that those appointed as parliamentary secretaries really could not express any determined adversity to such a suggestion but as for myself I cannot accept that proposal as appropriate having regard to all the circumstances. The hon. gentleman said that good men should be chosen on the basis of a full-time job. The hon. gentleman served in the capacity of parliamentary assistant and I think he would modestly allow himself to come within the ambit of the descriptive words "good men". He served for that amount and at no time in those days did I ever hear him suggest that an additional amount should be paid. I cannot believe that the hon. gentleman was too serious in that suggestion. I believe he was advancing a general argument as to the remuneration that goes to those in public life and not endeavouring seriously to advocate that at this time there should be such an increase.
In that connection may I say that those who serve in public life and who accept such responsibilities do so in the largest possible degree on the basis of the service they can render. I know of no one who enters public life in return for the compensation which appertains to the holding of public position.

Indeed, I have often said of hon. members of the House of Commons-and I am looking now at the hon. gentleman directly opposite .-how many of them, had they chosen to stay in private life, would find themselves today much better off monetarily speaking than is the case. It is true that if we cannot recruit through the public service the best men, even though the remuneration is not that which could be expected in private life, to serve with the same devotion they would bring to their private activities, then public life would indeed be the poorer as the result.
There is no suggestion of there being any hidden purpose in this legislation. The question of handling it in this fashion rather than doing what is done through the medium of an estimate answers itself.
I listened to the arguments of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on another subject and with that convincing power he exhibits on some occasions he was able to convince me that there were no sound reasons why the appointments in question should not be by legislative enactment directly rather than through the backdoor method of an estimate voted annually. In so far as the term is concerned, may I again say there is no question of the kind of representation that has been suggested here.
As for the hon. member for Essex East, I was glad to see the degree to which he showed an interest in the assurance that all important parts of Ontario shall be represented. Well, as a matter of fact it did. We know the Prime Minister used the term and I objected to this method but not with respect to parliamentary assistants. It seems to me that the really objectionable thing in our present situation is that the government chooses to appoint ministers of the crown by what the Prime Minister sees fit to refer to as the backdoor method. To that I take the same exception as I did a year ago. I think it is highly objectionable that ministers of the crown should be remunerated by an item in the estimates, but I never shared the views of Mr. Knowles when he was here that an appropriation act was not just as good legislation as any other kind. Perhaps it is not as convenient for lawyers to refer to but it is just as good legislation.
It seems to me, so far as parliamentary secretaries are concerned who do not share in the collective responsibility of the government and are not members of the government, that if the government chooses to legislate for their remuneration in the estimates through the appropriation act or chooses to do it this way, is a matter of relative indifference. I think on balance it is slightly better to do it this way. But I do think-and I would not have introduced the

Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries matter if the Prime Minister had not-it is very objectionable indeed to have ministers of the crown remunerated through the estimates and I do hope that before the session is over, if the Prime Minister continues to have ministers without portfolio whose utility some of us have some doubt about, it would be desirable to provide proper legislation for the purpose.
But what I rose to say-and it is very presumptuous of me to take issue with the Prime Minister in this-is that I think the Prime Minister was wrong when he said that parliamentary assistants in the past were appointed for a year at a time. The Prime Minister read the estimate. It is true that the remuneration was provided one year at a time but it is my understanding-and I saw many of the orders in council, though not all of them-that there was no term ever put in the orders in council. It would be my opinion-and I give this opinion without asking a fee because I am only a law student and not a lawyer-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the practice has now been established in the consideration of this bill in committee of dealing with 

clauses 1 and 2 together, therefore, I propose to follow that course because I have something to say not only on clause 1 but more particularly on clause 2 with which the Prime Minister and others have already dealt.
So far as the Prime Minister's argument about the nature of the previous appointments being for one year and one year only is concerned, I think he was wrong. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has pointed out, the impression created by this legislation is that the appointments are to be made for one year only though, of course, they may be renewed. The Prime Minister pointed out that that is not the intention of the bill. Then he brought forward the analogies to prove that he was right in his own interpretation. Yet I would point out to him that members of the government are appointed under I believe a statute but their salaries have to be voted each year in the estimates. If those salaries were not voted each year it would not affect their positions as ministers of the crown in any way, shape or form. I believe that would be the case in connection with this legislation, as my hon. friend has pointed out, unless the order in council specifies to the contrary, it would be of an indefinite character or for one year, whichever was expressed in the order in council. In our day when we appointed parliamentary assistants there certainly was no suggestion that the appointments should be made for one year only and I would be very surprised indeed if it were found that the orders in council passed at that time had that effect.
Certainly this legislation on the face of it seems to provide for a contrary practice and we on this side think that that is bad. Indeed, the Prime Minister himself, when he was speaking a few moments ago used these words, and I took them down as he said them, that the procedure in this bill was adopted so that each one-and by "each one" he meant each parliamentary secretary-will realize that he is appointed for the year. That is what we think is wrong in this legislation. Of course, there are other features of the legislation, in clause 2, particularly, which might be criticized. We are proceeding not by estimate but by legislation and though an item in the estimates-as my hon. friend who has just spoken has pointed out-is in a sense, I think, proceeding by legislation, nevertheless it is a more flexible form of legislation. When we pass a special bill for the appointment of parliamentary secretaries, as we are proposing to do now, it means that if at any time, for instance, the government

of the day wished to add one more parliamentary secretary to the 16, or two more or three more, that could only be done by an act of parliament.
As we see it-I do not see how there can be any other interpretation-this bill does provide for the principle of rotation in the appointment of parliamentary secretaries, and it is that to which we take exception.
If rotation is good as a principle in connection with the appointment of parliamentary secretaries, surely, Mr. Chairman, it might be argued that it is equally good as a principle to apply even to cabinet ministers, because some of the advantages of rotation which my right hon. friend has mentioned, not on this occasion but on a previous occasion, surely would attach to other appointments; but I do not think it is good. I think it would be a bad practice to appoint parliamentary secretaries for one year only. The clause states:
A parliamentary secretary shall he appointed to hold office for a period not exceeding 12 months-
As the Prime Minister indicated the other day, the main purpose behind the appointment of parliamentary secretaries-and it is a good purpose-is to relieve ministers of some of the burdens they are carrying. I have had, of course, some experience in office and I have had some experience-and a very happy experience it has been-in working with parliamentary secretaries. My last parliamentary secretary, my colleague sitting just behind me, has spoken on this matter and perhaps I should interpolate at this point to say that when my hon. friend from Richelieu-Vercheres talked about the possible desirability of increasing the salaries of parliamentary secretaries he was making the argument that if those positions are to be full time, not for one year only but for full time; if they are to be of that character, then perhaps $4,000 a year was not enough; that is, to pay a parliamentary secretary who was doing full-time work for his minister, which was not the situation in previous times.
He went on to say that if, however, the position of parliamentary secretary was not that kind of position, and if it became the kind of position we have in mind it may be under this legislation which provides for a one-year appointment only, then perhaps $4,000 a year might be too much. Perhaps it would be too much. If a parliamentary secretary is appointed for one year only, how can he really learn the work of his department during a period so short as that? I know from my own experience, and I am sure my hon. friends on this side who have been parliamentary assistants will agree with me, that it takes a parliamentary assistant
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries at least six months to become familiar with the work of his department to the point where he can really carry part of the ministerial burden. If he knows he is only going to be in office as a parliamentary secretary for one year, I do not think you can assume he is going to be able to do that part of the work which the minister would want him to do. This is our main criticism of this part of the legislation.
I suggest that perhaps an appointment of this kind, and there might be 16 appointed so that in four years there would be 64 of them, would be a kind of political scholarship to be awarded by the Prime Minister to some of his more deserving colleagues. I suggest that political scholarships might more properly be awarded by the Canada Council which has been set up for the purpose of awarding scholarships. If the Prime Minister replies to this argument by saying, well, there is no objection to reappointment and perhaps we should assume that they will be reappointed, my answer to that would be that this legislation says the appointment shall be for a period not exceeding 12 months. Surely, that is the assumption in the legislation, and if the parliamentary secretary feels that the only chance he has of continuing in his job is to become valuable in his job, that will not give him a sense of security and achievement in his work which he will need to have if he is going to do the job which the government no doubt had in mind in appointing him in the first place.
Now there is another objection and it is, I think, quite a strong one to the appointment for one year only. I touched on this a few moments ago. A parliamentary assistant not only has to assist the minister in the house and out of the house, but he must also become familiar with the official work of the department. This means he has to establish a close, and I would hope constructive relationship with the deputy minister and the senior officials. It is not going to be any encouragement, though perhaps encouragement is not the right word, to the senior officials of the department to work as closely with the parliamentary assistant as they should, and it is not going to be much encouragement for the parliamentary assistant to work closely with the senior officials if he should feel that by the end of the year his scholarship will be over and someone else will be taking over from him. We think, therefore, Mr. Chairman, that this particular provision of the legislation is not designed to enable the government to fulfil the functions which they had in mind, so we were told, in introducing this legislation in the first place.
This will, of course, relieve the Prime Minister of one difficulty. He will now have

The governor in council may make regulations providing for the payment to a parliamentary secretary of reasonable travelling and other expenses
(a)	incurred by him in the discharge of his duties during a session of parliament while away from Ottawa, or
(b)	incurred by him in the discharge of his duties while away from his ordinary place of residence during a period when parliament is not in session.
I do not think it was at any time ever the expectation that the parliamentary secretary should remain in Ottawa during the entire year. The appointment would be for a period of a year, or in the words of the estimate to which I referred earlier, there would be a salary of $4,000 per annum and pro rata for any period less than a year. At no time did parliamentary assistants reside in Ottawa during the entire year. There were times when they returned, and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres will corroborate this, to Ottawa after the session. speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MORTGAGES, CERTIFICATES, PILOTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I could have the floor for a moment because I intend, with the hon. members' permission, to ask for the adjournment of debate on this bill for the following reason. Last evening the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) suggested that there should be a firm and general basis of agreement with the United States regarding pilotage on the great lakes before the Canadian legislation dealing with this matter is finally made effective. In fact there have been extensive consultations with the United States authorities on this matter already and numerous meetings have been held. Of the two most important points involved, we have already reached agreement with the United States on one; that is, the reciprocal recognition of pilotage certificates or licences which might be issued by the authorities of either country. However, there has not been firm agreement as yet as to the basis upon which pilotage requirements should apply in the waters of the great lakes and the areas which should be involved. The reason for this is, I understand, largely because the United States has not yet reached an internal decision on this matter, although we in Canada have reached a tentative decision as to the solution we favour.
While the legislation proposed in this bill is sufficiently general to permit this matter to be worked out satisfactorily within its terms, I am quite prepared to see another attempt made to reach agreement with the United States authorities on this additional point, and indeed will make arrangements myself at the earliest opportunity to visit Washington for discussion of this subject. I would therefore ask the hon. member for Laurier who has the floor if he would be good enough to move the adjournment of the debate.

However, my hope last evening was, and still is, that a committee from Canada and the United States be established and that an agreement be worked out so that such agreement can come back to the house.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES

speakeroldname: Hon. George H. Hees (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: the second reading of Bill C-38, to make provision for the reduction of certain class and commodity rates on freight traffic.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker when the house was discussing this matter last evening at another stage, namely the resolution stage, I indicated that I should like to make some additional remarks on second reading of the bill. I am prepared to make those remarks now, not with the intention of delaying this legislation but because of comments which were made earlier on the subject by others.
Before I come to that, may I say that this measure, Bill C-38, an act to make provision for the reduction of certain class and commodity rates on freight traffic, is, on the face of it, simple enough. The pertinent and governing clause is, of course, clause 3 and it can be divided under several heads. By virtue of clause 3, the board:
1.	Shall make an order.
2.	Shall revise class and commodity rates other than competitive rates of railway companies.

3.	Shall revise them downward as they were increased by the judgment-the 17 per cent case-so that in the opinion of the board the estimated aggregate gross revenues of the companies will be reduced by $20 million.
That is the effective clause. Clause 4 provides for the payments to be made out of the consolidated revenue fund. Clauses 5 and 6 I do not think are in the slightest degree contentious, and clause 7 is inserted in the bill so there shall be no conflict between the Railway Act and this act. Under clause 7 the board may allow a reduction in the select territory or in the rates subject to the Maritime Freight Rates Act only to meet reductions in the cost of operations. It is now stated that a payment to a railway company under the new statute shall be deemed to be a reduction in the case of the railway operations. But I shall go back to clause 3, which, in my opinion, is the only one that can in any way be considered to be contentious, and I ask the house and the minister to consider the words in line 18 of clause 3, "increased by 17 per cent". The clause reads:
Forthwith upon the coming into force of this act, the board shall by order require the companies to revise such of their class rates and commodity rates (other than competitive rates) in effect at the commencement of this act as were, pursuant to order No. 96300, increased by 17 per cent.
The point I am making is this: supposing the railways were unable to increase their rates by 17 per cent, and there was evidence of this placed before the board. Suppose the railways were able to increase their rates by only 10 per cent or by only 3 per cent, because that is all the traffic would bear? I point out that there are a number of cases, as was stated in the evidence given before the board of transport commissioners, in which the 17 per cent increase could not be wholly put into effect. What happens then? Does it mean that in these rates there would be a consequent reduction of 7 per cent?
I think we are entitled to clarification. In other words, will this rate or these rates, where the full effect of the 17 per cent has not been felt because of the conditions I have mentioned, enjoy the full effect of the subsidy? I leave that to go to another equally contentious point in my opinion.
The minister has said that the government does not propose to permit any further general increase in freight rates pending the decision or the study made by the royal commission. I do not think I am incorrectly quoting the minister but if he feels I am I will quote from the statement he made. The minister having said that, I ask him this question. Is he or the house familiar with section 328 (5) of the Railway Act?

I ask the house to listen to these words. That section reads as follows:
-the powers given to the board under this act to fix, determine and enforce just and reasonable rates, and to change and alter rates as changing conditions or cost of transportation may from time to time require, are not limited or in any manner affected by the provisions of any act of the parliament of Canada-
This means that when an application is before the board of transport commissioners for determination it is their duty and responsibility to hear the case. There is no other act of parliament which can prevent the board from doing that. A fortiori, there is therefore no statement that may be made by the minister, the government or the Prime Minister which can stop the board of transport commissioners from hearing the case.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: That is right.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Having said that, where does that lead the board of transport commissioners? How can the board in any way be affected by the statement the minister has made. Unfortunately I cannot locate the statement at the moment.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: May I answer the hon. member at this time?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member knows only too well the government has no right at all to interfere with the board of transport commissioners either hearing the case or bringing down a judgment. The government has no intention of doing either of those things. However, when a freight rate award is appealed to the governor in council, the governor in council has the option of either allowing of disallowing the increase that has been made by the board.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: I was coming to that point, Mr. Speaker. That is not what the minister said.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: That is what the minister meant.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
But what the minister said and what he meant are two different things. If the board of transport commissioners are going to be allowed to hear the case-and having made a determination an appeal may be made under section 53 (1) of the Railway Act-that is one matter. The minister I am sure gave careful consideration to the statement he made because if my recollection is right he put it on Hansard on more than one occasion. What I am complaining about now is that, by inference, that statement is a direction to the board or perhaps, it is a direction to the Canadian National Railways not to proceed with the application which is now before the board.
Freight Rates

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext: It is intended to be neither, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Of course, the minister did not make that clear. On the contrary what was said was not at all in accordance either with what I am saying now or with what the minister has said within the last few moments. In order to make the thing quite clear what the minister should have said was this: "We are not going to interfere with the application now before the board but when the order is appealed by the provinces or by any other group we will hear that application under section 53 (1) of the act and decide against it." The minister has closed the door, however, by saying there is going to be no further increase. If it is found that within the period of a year the wages of the railway workers have increased and it becomes necessary because of changing conditions in Canada to increase these wages, then the minister and the government are stopped from giving to those workers a further increase because of the statement which has been made.
Turning now to another matter, the bill, as I said, by means of clause 3 directs the board to make an order in accordance with the manner I have outlined earlier. This is the measure promised by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Green) when speaking as the acting prime minister in November, 1958 he said this was the measure designed to relieve against the discrimination which existed in freight rates and to relieve against inequalities including any that may be aggravated by the present increase in the amount of 17 per cent. The other measure is a royal commission the terms of which we have not yet got although the Prime Minister did indicate yesterday that its appointment would come before third reading.
We in this group and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) tried to get a further commitment from the Prime Minister to the effect that we might be able to discuss the terms of reference when the announcement was made. We were not successful in doing this notwithstanding the fact that when he made his statement in November, 1958 the then acting prime minister made it quite clear that the other measure he had in mind- whether it related to a royal commission or another inquiry was not made clear at the time-would result in the consideration of railway problems and railway policy. He indicated that the inquiry would consider not only a comprehensive statement of railway freight rates including the situation of the long haul provinces in the west and in the Atlantic region but also specific problems which require solution if Canada's railways are to serve the national interest without prejudicing particular industries and areas.

Freight Rates
The intention of the government at that time was quite clear. First, there would be an interim measure to deal with an immediate problem and, second, a royal commission to deal with the long term problem. What we have before us now is the long awaited measure to relieve against the freight rate increase. The intention of the government is to provide immediate alleviation by means of this measure. I would like to know what this bill means and to what extent it provides immediate alleviation.
The bill clearly excludes from the operation of the subsidy the whole field of competitive rates and, while it is not stated, it also excludes the following items, since the board of transport commissioners in their judgment excepted these from its operation in the 17 per cent case: agreed charges, international rates, import and export rates, grain and grain products in western Canada, and grain and grain products from prairie points to Vancouver, Prince Rupert and other parts of British Columbia. It excludes those new piggy-back rates which are now important, and I presume that other rates are also excluded. Hence the bill applies to a very limited field in the freight rate structure.
In his statement earlier the minister indicated that the reduction would be one in the neighbourhood of seven per cent, in that the subsidy would be applied in such a way that rates generally, as applied in the judgment, would be reduced from 17 per cent to 10 per cent. But a question which arises and which I think is of importance is this: What freight revenues of the carriers will be affected by this measure? I think We should be told what they will be. The minister has not said so, but I would venture to say that only a very small fraction of the freight revenues of the railways, and incidentally of the freight rates which the west and the Atlantic provinces will have to pay, is affected by this decision. My reason for saying this is that of all those exceptions the class and commodity rates are getting now to be smaller and smaller and every time there is an increase in freight rates the effect of it is made to be felt upon a lesser and lesser group of rates and therefore it becomes a greater burden for those who have to pay those rates and they are affected more seriously by it.
I come now to the question which was asked earlier and which I will not go into in detail at this stage, but on which I hope, when the bill is referred to the committee, there will be some clarification. I refer to the method by which this order is going to become operative. Yesterday and earlier I
asked the question, what formula is going to be adopted? What method is the board going to establish? What procedure is going to be followed in the implementation of this subsidy of $20 million? How is it going to be distributed? Is the relief granted by this measure to be tied up with wage increases? The minister said no and then later on he said that it was not going to be tied up with anything. Well, it has to be tied up with something. There has to be some kind of formula under which the board is going to proceed, and I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it is not going to be nearly as easy as anticipated by the minister because those of us who are familiar with the bridge subsidy of $7 million, which is administered by the board of transport commissioners, know that there was no easy method to put that into effect.
The railways have said all along that they need the relief granted by the 17 per cent increase. They said that they needed all of this increase in rates to put them in funds so as to accept and put into effect the majority report of the conciliation board. I think the house should be told whether this bill is subsidizing wages. If so, the minister should tell us. Not only would this create a precedent but it could have serious implications for the future.
There is another matter which I would like to discuss at this time but I would prefer not to begin its discussion and have it interrupted; therefore, sir, I wonder whether you would call it six o'clock?
On motion of Mr. Chevrier the debate was adjourned.
